slides.heading: The fuels in the pipeline
slides.body_md: Part 1 — Natural gas, biogas and CNG are mostly **methane**; LPG is mainly propane and butane. These are **alkanes**, the simplest family of hydrocarbons. We learn how methane and ethane are made in the laboratory and how they react.

visual.alt: Table of three everyday fuels, the alkanes in them and where they are used

slides.narration: Namaste! The gas that runs many city buses, the biogas made from cow dung and the gas piped into kitchens are all mostly methane. The gas in a cooking cylinder is a mixture of propane and butane. All of these are alkanes. In this part we study the first two alkanes, methane and ethane: how to make them and how they react.

slides.heading: Alkanes: the saturated family
slides.body_md: **Alkanes** are saturated hydrocarbons: every carbon–carbon bond is a **single** bond. General formula **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**: methane CH₄ (n = 1), ethane C₂H₆ (n = 2), propane C₃H₈ (n = 3). With no double or triple bond to open up, alkanes are **fairly unreactive**: they burn, and they undergo **substitution** with chlorine, but they do not add other molecules.

slides.narration: Alkanes contain only single bonds between their carbon atoms, so we call them saturated. Each member has two more hydrogen atoms than twice its number of carbon atoms. Because there is no double or triple bond, alkanes are rather unreactive. Their two important reactions are burning in air and swapping hydrogen atoms for chlorine atoms.

slides.heading: Methane: a greenhouse gas of concern
slides.body_md: Methane is released by **paddy fields**, **cattle** (digestion), **landfills** and rotting waste, **coal mines** and leaks from **natural-gas** pipelines. Like carbon dioxide, it **absorbs infrared radiation** given off by the Earth and so **traps heat**. Molecule for molecule it traps **far more heat** than carbon dioxide (roughly 25–30 times over a century), so even small amounts add to **global warming**.

slides.narration: Methane escapes into the air from flooded rice fields, from the stomachs of cattle, from rotting rubbish and from leaking gas pipes. Like carbon dioxide, it soaks up heat given off by the Earth and keeps the atmosphere warm. In fact each molecule of methane traps much more heat than a molecule of carbon dioxide, which is why it is a greenhouse gas of real concern.

slides.heading: Methane from sodium ethanoate
slides.body_md: Heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with **soda lime** (sodium hydroxide + calcium oxide) removes CO₂ from it as sodium carbonate — **decarboxylation** — and gives an alkane with **one carbon fewer**. Sodium ethanoate (sodium acetate) gives methane. **Calcium oxide** keeps the sodium hydroxide dry and stops it from attacking the glass; it does not take part in the reaction.

visual.alt: Sodium ethanoate plus sodium hydroxide, heated with calcium oxide, gives methane and sodium carbonate
visual.caption: Decarboxylation: the alkane has one carbon atom fewer than the salt.

slides.narration: To make methane, sodium ethanoate is heated with soda lime, a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide. The sodium hydroxide takes away carbon dioxide from the salt as sodium carbonate, leaving methane. This is called decarboxylation, and the alkane always has one carbon atom fewer than the salt. The calcium oxide simply keeps the sodium hydroxide dry and protects the glass.

slides.heading: Laboratory preparation of methane
slides.body_md: A dry mixture of sodium ethanoate and soda lime (about 1 : 3) is heated in a **hard glass test tube**, clamped with its mouth slightly lower than its base so that any moisture does not run back onto the hot glass. Methane is **collected over water** (downward displacement of water) because it is **nearly insoluble in water**. It is a colourless, odourless gas, lighter than air.

slides.narration: In the laboratory, a dry mixture of sodium ethanoate and soda lime is heated strongly in a hard glass test tube. The tube is tilted slightly downward so that moisture cannot run back and crack the hot glass. Methane hardly dissolves in water, so it is collected by letting it push water out of an upside down gas jar standing in a trough.

slides.heading: Ethane from sodium propanoate; alkanes from alkyl halides
slides.body_md: **Ethane** is made the same way from **sodium propanoate**. Alkanes also form when an alkyl halide is **reduced** by **nascent hydrogen**, [H], produced from a **zinc–copper couple** and ethanol: iodomethane gives methane and bromoethane gives ethane.

visual.alt: Table of four methods of preparing methane and ethane with reagents, products and equations

slides.narration: Ethane is made in the same way as methane, by heating sodium propanoate with soda lime. There is a second route too. An alkyl halide is reduced by freshly made, or nascent, hydrogen from a zinc and copper couple in ethanol. The halogen atom is replaced by hydrogen, so iodomethane gives methane and bromoethane gives ethane.

slides.heading: Worked example: mass of ethane from its salt
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 9.6 g of sodium propanoate, C₂H₅COONa, is heated with excess soda lime. Find the mass of ethane formed. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23)

**Step 1.** Molar mass of C₂H₅COONa: $3 \times 12 + 5 \times 1 + 2 \times 16 + 23 = 96$ g.

**Step 2.** Moles of salt: $\frac{9.6}{96} = 0.1$ mol.

**Step 3.** One mole of salt gives one mole of ethane (C₂H₆, 30 g), so mass of ethane $= 0.1 \times 30 = 3$ g.

visual.alt: Sodium propanoate plus sodium hydroxide, heated with calcium oxide, gives ethane and sodium carbonate
visual.caption: 1 mol of salt gives 1 mol of ethane.

slides.narration: First find the molar mass of sodium propanoate: three carbons, five hydrogens, two oxygens and one sodium make ninety six grams. So nine point six grams is one tenth of a mole. The equation shows that each mole of the salt gives one mole of ethane, which weighs thirty grams. One tenth of that is three grams of ethane.

slides.heading: Combustion: complete and incomplete
slides.body_md:
In **plenty of air**, alkanes burn with a **blue, non-sooty flame** to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing much heat — so they are good **fuels**. In a **limited supply of air**, combustion is **incomplete**: poisonous **carbon monoxide** (and soot) form.

- CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
- 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O (limited air)
- 2C₂H₆ + 5O₂ → 4CO + 6H₂O (limited air)

visual.alt: Two ethane plus seven oxygen gives four carbon dioxide plus six water
visual.caption: Complete combustion of ethane in excess air.

slides.narration: With plenty of air, methane and ethane burn with a clean blue flame, forming carbon dioxide and water and giving out a lot of heat. That is why they are used as fuels. If the air supply is poor, burning is incomplete, and carbon monoxide and soot are formed. Carbon monoxide is poisonous, so gas heaters must never be used in a closed room.

slides.heading: Worked example: volumes of gases in combustion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 50 cm³ of methane is burnt completely in oxygen. Find the volume of oxygen used and of carbon dioxide formed, all volumes at the same temperature and pressure.

**Step 1.** Equation: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. By Gay-Lussac's law, gas volumes are in the ratio of the coefficients: 1 : 2 : 1.

**Step 2.** Oxygen: $50 \times 2 = 100$ cm³.

**Step 3.** Carbon dioxide: $50 \times 1 = 50$ cm³. (Water condenses to a liquid at room temperature.)

visual.alt: Table of the volumes of methane, oxygen and carbon dioxide in the combustion of fifty cubic centimetres of methane

slides.narration: Write the balanced equation first: one methane and two oxygen give one carbon dioxide and two water. For gases at the same temperature and pressure, volumes react in the same simple ratio as the coefficients. So fifty cubic centimetres of methane needs twice that, one hundred, of oxygen, and forms fifty of carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Substitution with chlorine
slides.body_md:
In **diffused sunlight**, chlorine **replaces** the hydrogen atoms of methane **one at a time** — a **substitution** reaction typical of saturated compounds. Each step gives off HCl:

- CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (chloromethane)
- CH₃Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl (dichloromethane)
- CH₂Cl₂ + Cl₂ → CHCl₃ + HCl (trichloromethane, chloroform)
- CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl (tetrachloromethane, carbon tetrachloride)

In the dark there is no reaction; in **direct** sunlight the mixture explodes. Ethane reacts in the same way: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl.

slides.narration: Methane and chlorine do nothing in the dark. In diffused sunlight, chlorine atoms replace the hydrogen atoms of methane one at a time, giving off hydrogen chloride at each step. The products are chloromethane, dichloromethane, trichloromethane, which is chloroform, and finally carbon tetrachloride. Ethane reacts in the same way to give chloroethane first. In bright direct sunlight the mixture can explode.

slides.heading: Uses of methane and ethane
slides.body_md: Methane and ethane burn cleanly and give a lot of heat, so their main use is as **fuels**. They are also **raw materials** for the chemical industry.

slides.narration: Because they burn cleanly and release a lot of heat, methane and ethane are mostly used as fuels, in natural gas, compressed natural gas and biogas. Methane is also used to make hydrogen and carbon black, the black filler in tyres and printing ink. Ethane is heated in industry to make ethene, the starting material for many plastics.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Alkanes: saturated, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; methane and ethane are the first two.
Methane traps heat strongly: a greenhouse gas from paddy fields, cattle, landfills and gas leaks.
Sodium ethanoate or sodium propanoate + soda lime → methane or ethane (one carbon fewer).
Iodomethane or bromoethane + nascent hydrogen (Zn–Cu couple, ethanol) → methane or ethane.
Complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O; limited air gives CO. Chlorine substitutes H atoms one at a time in diffused sunlight.

visual.alt: Summary table of three reactions with their type and condition

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, and methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. Methane and ethane are made by heating sodium salts with soda lime, or by reducing alkyl halides with nascent hydrogen. They burn completely to carbon dioxide and water, or incompletely to carbon monoxide. With chlorine in diffused sunlight they undergo substitution.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Always write the condition over the arrow: soda lime and heat; Zn–Cu couple; diffused sunlight.
Decarboxylation: the alkane has one carbon fewer than the sodium salt.
Say "diffused sunlight" for chlorination; dark gives no reaction, direct sunlight an explosion.

rows: Methane collected by upward displacement of air
Collected over water: it is nearly insoluble

Check the balancing of ethane combustion, which needs two ethane and seven oxygen. And for chlorination, say diffused sunlight, because there is no reaction in the dark and an explosion in bright sunlight.

These **unsaturated** hydrocarbons are made by **removing** small molecules from saturated compounds, and they react by **adding** molecules across the multiple bond.

slides.narration: Ethene has a double bond between its two carbon atoms, and ethyne has a triple bond. They are unsaturated. In the laboratory they are made by removing small molecules such as water or hydrogen bromide from saturated compounds. And their typical reactions do the reverse: other molecules add across the double or triple bond.

slides.heading: Ethene from bromoethane: dehydrohalogenation
slides.body_md: Boiling **bromoethane** with a concentrated solution of **potassium hydroxide in ethanol** (alcoholic KOH) removes **one H atom and one Br atom** from neighbouring carbon atoms as HBr. This is **dehydrohalogenation** (here dehydrobromination). Note: **aqueous** KOH gives ethanol instead, not ethene.

spec.equation: C2H5Br + KOH ->[{alcohol, heat}] C2H4 + KBr + H2O

visual.alt: Bromoethane plus potassium hydroxide in alcohol, heated, gives ethene, potassium bromide and water
visual.caption: Alcoholic KOH removes H and Br from neighbouring carbons.

slides.narration: Ethene can be made from bromoethane by boiling it with potassium hydroxide dissolved in alcohol. A hydrogen atom from one carbon and the bromine atom from the next carbon are removed together, and a double bond forms between the two carbons. The reaction is called dehydrohalogenation. Be careful: with potassium hydroxide dissolved in water, bromoethane gives ethanol instead.

slides.heading: Ethene from ethanol: dehydration
slides.body_md:
Ethanol is heated with **excess concentrated sulphuric acid** at about **170 °C**. The acid is a **dehydrating agent**: it removes a molecule of water from each ethanol molecule. The gas is passed through **sodium hydroxide solution** to remove the impurities sulphur dioxide and carbon dioxide, and is collected **over water**.

C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O (conc. H₂SO₄, 170 °C)

nodes.label: Wash gas in NaOH solution (removes SO₂, CO₂)

visual.alt: Flow of the preparation of ethene from ethanol: heat with concentrated sulphuric acid, wash the gas in sodium hydroxide, collect over water

slides.narration: Ethene can also be made by heating ethanol with excess concentrated sulphuric acid to about one hundred and seventy degrees Celsius. The acid pulls a molecule of water out of each ethanol molecule. Some of the acid is reduced to sulphur dioxide, so the gas is washed in sodium hydroxide solution to remove acidic gases, and then collected over water.

slides.heading: Quick check: preparing ethene
slides.body_md: Choose the reagent that converts a given compound into ethene.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ethene can be made by removing hydrogen bromide from bromoethane or water from ethanol. Decide which reagent removes which small molecule, and remember that the solvent matters: potassium hydroxide in alcohol behaves differently from potassium hydroxide in water.

slides.heading: Ethyne from calcium carbide
slides.body_md:
Water is dropped slowly from a dropping funnel onto lumps of **calcium carbide**. Ethyne is given off at once and **collected over water**; the residue is calcium hydroxide. Water is added **drop by drop** because the reaction is fast and gives out much heat.

CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂

Pure ethyne is almost odourless; gas from commercial carbide smells of **garlic** because of impurities such as phosphine.

slides.narration: In the laboratory, water is dripped onto lumps of calcium carbide in a flask. Ethyne bubbles off straight away and is collected over water, and calcium hydroxide is left behind. The water is added slowly because the reaction is rapid and very hot. Gas made from impure carbide smells of garlic, but this smell comes from impurities, not from ethyne itself.

slides.heading: Ethyne from 1,2-dibromoethane
slides.body_md: **1,2-dibromoethane** (CH₂Br–CH₂Br) has a bromine atom on each carbon. Boiling it with **alcoholic potassium hydroxide** removes **two** molecules of HBr, one after the other, and leaves a **triple bond**: CH₂Br–CH₂Br → CH≡CH. This is a double dehydrohalogenation.

visual.alt: One two dibromoethane plus two potassium hydroxide in alcohol gives ethyne, two potassium bromide and two water
visual.caption: Two molecules of HBr are removed from each molecule.

slides.narration: One two dibromoethane has a bromine atom on each of its two carbon atoms. Boiling it with alcoholic potassium hydroxide removes hydrogen bromide twice. After the first removal a double bond forms; after the second, a triple bond. So the final product is ethyne, along with potassium bromide and water.

slides.heading: Worked example: reagents and conditions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the reagent and condition, and write the equation, for (a) ethanol → ethene; (b) bromoethane → ethene; (c) 1,2-dibromoethane → ethyne.

**(a)** Excess conc. H₂SO₄, about 170 °C: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O.

**(b)** Alcoholic KOH, boil: C₂H₅Br + KOH → C₂H₄ + KBr + H₂O.

**(c)** Alcoholic KOH, boil: C₂H₄Br₂ + 2KOH → C₂H₂ + 2KBr + 2H₂O.

**Check.** Count atoms of each element on both sides of every equation.

visual.alt: Table of three preparations with the small molecule removed and the reagent used

slides.narration: Ask what must be removed. To turn ethanol into ethene, water is removed, so we need a dehydrating agent, concentrated sulphuric acid. To turn bromoethane into ethene, hydrogen bromide is removed by alcoholic potassium hydroxide. One two dibromoethane loses hydrogen bromide twice to give ethyne, so two units of potassium hydroxide are needed.

slides.heading: Quick check: preparing ethyne
slides.body_md: Identify the products of a reaction that gives ethyne.
slides.narration: Quick check. Calcium carbide reacts with water to give ethyne. Think about what is left of the calcium, and remember that a metal oxide that meets water usually ends up as a hydroxide. Then match both products to the options.

slides.heading: Addition of hydrogen
slides.body_md:
Unsaturated hydrocarbons undergo **addition** reactions: atoms add across the multiple bond, which becomes a single bond. With **hydrogen**, in the presence of finely divided **nickel** at about 300 °C (hydrogenation):

- C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ (ethene → ethane)
- C₂H₂ + H₂ → C₂H₄, then C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆

Overall, ethyne adds **two** molecules of hydrogen.

visual.alt: Ethyne plus two hydrogen over nickel at about three hundred degrees gives ethane
visual.caption: Ethyne adds hydrogen in two steps, through ethene.

slides.narration: Because ethene and ethyne have spare bonds, other molecules can add across them. With hydrogen, over a nickel catalyst at about three hundred degrees Celsius, ethene becomes ethane. Ethyne first becomes ethene and then ethane, so overall it adds two molecules of hydrogen. Adding hydrogen in this way is called hydrogenation.

slides.heading: Addition of halogens
slides.body_md:
Chlorine, bromine and iodine add across C=C and C≡C at room temperature, with **no sunlight needed**.

- C₂H₄ + Cl₂ → C₂H₄Cl₂ (1,2-dichloroethane)
- C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ (1,2-dibromoethane)
- C₂H₄ + I₂ → C₂H₄I₂ (1,2-diiodoethane)
- C₂H₂ + 2Br₂ → C₂H₂Br₄ (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane); with chlorine, 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane

Ethene adds **one** molecule of halogen; ethyne adds **two**.

Chlorine gives one two dichloroethane, bromine gives one two dibromoethane, and iodine gives one two diiodoethane, with one halogen atom on each carbon. Ethyne adds two molecules of halogen, so with bromine it ends up with two bromine atoms on each carbon.

slides.heading: Worked example: how much bromine?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** What mass of bromine adds completely to (a) 1.4 g of ethene, (b) 1.3 g of ethyne? (C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80)

**(a)** C₂H₄ = 28 g mol⁻¹: $\frac{1.4}{28} = 0.05$ mol. One Br₂ per C₂H₄: $0.05 \times 160 = 8$ g of bromine.

**(b)** C₂H₂ = 26 g mol⁻¹: $\frac{1.3}{26} = 0.05$ mol. Two Br₂ per C₂H₂: $0.05 \times 2 \times 160 = 16$ g of bromine.

visual.alt: Table comparing the bromine needed by equal numbers of moles of ethene and ethyne

slides.narration: Change each mass into moles. One point four grams of ethene is five hundredths of a mole, and so is one point three grams of ethyne. Each mole of ethene adds one mole of bromine, which weighs one hundred and sixty grams, so eight grams are needed. Ethyne adds two moles of bromine per mole, so it needs twice as much: sixteen grams.

slides.heading: Test for unsaturation
slides.body_md:
Bubble the gas into **bromine water** (or bromine dissolved in tetrachloromethane), which is **orange-brown**.

- **Ethene or ethyne**: the colour disappears at once — bromine **adds** across the multiple bond to give colourless products.
- **Ethane or methane**: the colour **stays** (in the dark there is no substitution, and alkanes cannot add bromine).

This distinguishes **saturated** from **unsaturated** hydrocarbons.

slides.heading: Uses of ethene and ethyne
slides.body_md: Ethene and ethyne are important raw materials, and ethyne gives one of the hottest flames known.

rows: Making polythene; making ethanol and other chemicals; ripening fruit (a natural plant hormone)
Oxy-acetylene flame (about 3000 °C) for welding and cutting metals; making plastics such as PVC; lighting in old carbide lamps

slides.narration: Ethene is the starting material for polythene and for making ethanol, and in small amounts it helps fruits to ripen, since plants produce it naturally. Ethyne burnt in pure oxygen gives the oxy acetylene flame, hot enough to weld and cut steel. It was also once burnt in carbide lamps used by miners.

notes.title: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Alkynes — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Alkanes; methane as a greenhouse gas
sections.body_md:
**Alkanes** are saturated hydrocarbons (only C–C single bonds), general formula **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**: methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀. They are fairly unreactive; their main reactions are **combustion** and **substitution**.

**Methane as a greenhouse gas.** Sources: flooded paddy fields, cattle, landfills and sewage, coal mines, leaks of natural gas. Methane absorbs the infrared radiation given off by the Earth and so traps heat; molecule for molecule it traps far more heat than carbon dioxide (roughly 25–30 times over a century). Rising methane levels add to **global warming**.

key_terms.definition_md: A saturated hydrocarbon with only single bonds between carbon atoms, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide or methane, that absorbs heat radiated by the Earth and keeps the atmosphere warm.

rows: Decay of plant matter without air

visual.alt: Table of three sources of methane and how it forms in each

sections.heading: 2. Preparation of methane and ethane
sections.body_md:
**Decarboxylation:** the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid heated with **soda lime** (NaOH + CaO) gives an alkane with **one carbon fewer** and sodium carbonate. CaO keeps the NaOH dry and protects the glass.

**Reduction of alkyl halides** by **nascent hydrogen** [H] from a zinc–copper couple and ethanol: the halogen atom is replaced by hydrogen.

**Laboratory method for methane:** heat a dry 1 : 3 mixture of sodium ethanoate and soda lime in a hard glass test tube (mouth slightly lower than the base); collect methane over water, as it is nearly insoluble in water.

key_terms.definition_md: Removal of carbon dioxide (as sodium carbonate) from the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid by heating with soda lime.
A mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide.
Freshly produced, very reactive hydrogen, written [H].

visual.alt: Table of four methods of preparing methane and ethane

sections.heading: 3. Combustion and substitution of methane and ethane
sections.body_md:
**Complete combustion** (excess air): blue, non-sooty flame; CO₂ and H₂O; much heat (fuels).
**Incomplete combustion** (limited air): poisonous **carbon monoxide** and soot.

**Substitution with chlorine** (diffused sunlight): H atoms replaced by Cl one at a time, HCl given off at each step: CH₃Cl (chloromethane) → CH₂Cl₂ (dichloromethane) → CHCl₃ (trichloromethane, chloroform) → CCl₄ (tetrachloromethane, carbon tetrachloride). Dark: no reaction. Direct sunlight: explosive (CH₄ + 2Cl₂ → C + 4HCl). Ethane: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl, and so on up to C₂Cl₆.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction in which an atom or group in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group, as when Cl replaces H in methane.
Burning in a limited supply of air, giving carbon monoxide and/or carbon instead of carbon dioxide.

visual.alt: Table of the four substitution products of methane with chlorine

sections.heading: 4. Preparation of ethene and ethyne
sections.body_md:
**Ethene (C₂H₄):**
- **Dehydrohalogenation:** bromoethane boiled with **alcoholic** KOH (aqueous KOH gives ethanol instead).
- **Dehydration:** ethanol heated with **excess conc. H₂SO₄** at about **170 °C**; the gas is washed in NaOH solution (removes SO₂ and CO₂) and collected over water.

**Ethyne (C₂H₂):**
- **Calcium carbide + water** (water added drop by drop; collected over water). Impure ethyne smells of garlic because of impurities such as phosphine; pure ethyne is almost odourless.
- **1,2-dibromoethane** boiled with **alcoholic** KOH: two HBr removed.

key_terms.definition_md: Removal of a hydrogen halide (such as HBr) from neighbouring carbon atoms of a compound, forming a multiple bond.
Removal of a molecule of water from a compound, as when ethanol forms ethene.

visual.alt: Table of the four preparations of ethene and ethyne

sections.heading: 5. Addition reactions and the test for unsaturation
sections.body_md:
Unsaturated hydrocarbons undergo **addition**: atoms add across the C=C or C≡C, which becomes a single bond. Ethene adds **one** molecule; ethyne adds **two**.

- **Hydrogen** (nickel, about 300 °C): ethene → ethane; ethyne → ethene → ethane.
- **Halogens** (room temperature, no light needed): ethene + Cl₂ → 1,2-dichloroethane; + Br₂ → 1,2-dibromoethane; + I₂ → 1,2-diiodoethane. Ethyne + 2Br₂ → 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane; + 2Cl₂ → 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane.

**Test for unsaturation:** orange-brown bromine water (or bromine in CCl₄) is **decolourised** by ethene and ethyne but **not** by ethane or methane.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction in which atoms add across a double or triple bond, so that one product forms and the multiple bond becomes a single bond.
Addition of hydrogen to an unsaturated compound, using a catalyst such as nickel.

visual.alt: Table of the bromine-water test on ethane, ethene and ethyne

sections.heading: 6. Uses of methane, ethane, ethene and ethyne
sections.body_md:
- **Methane:** fuel (natural gas, CNG, biogas); making hydrogen, carbon black (tyres, printing ink) and chloromethanes.
- **Ethane:** fuel; cracked to make ethene; making chloroethane.
- **Ethene:** making polythene; making ethanol; artificial ripening of fruit (a natural plant hormone).
- **Ethyne:** oxy-acetylene flame (about 3000 °C) for welding and cutting metals; making plastics such as PVC; carbide lamps.

key_terms.definition_md: The very hot flame obtained by burning ethyne (acetylene) in oxygen, used for welding and cutting metals.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that sodium ethanoate gives ethane (it gives methane: one carbon fewer).
- Forgetting the condition: soda lime and heat; Zn–Cu couple; diffused sunlight; alcoholic KOH; conc. H₂SO₄ at 170 °C; Ni at 300 °C.
- Using aqueous KOH for dehydrohalogenation.
- Writing ethyne + Br₂ → C₂H₂Br₂ when bromine is in excess (the product is C₂H₂Br₄).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Equation (1 mark): correct formulae, balanced, with the condition.
- Observation (1 mark): colour before and after ("orange-brown to colourless").
- Test to distinguish (2 marks): reagent, plus the observation for each compound.

questions.stem_md: Methane released from flooded paddy fields, cattle and landfill sites is a concern for the climate because methane:

options.text_md: destroys the ozone layer by releasing chlorine atoms
causes acid rain by forming sulphuric acid in clouds
is poisonous and is absorbed by green plants
traps heat radiated by the Earth, and molecule for molecule traps far more heat than carbon dioxide

questions.solution_md: Methane is a greenhouse gas that absorbs infrared radiation from the Earth; per molecule it is much stronger than CO₂ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the laboratory preparation of methane, sodium ethanoate is heated with soda lime. Soda lime is a mixture of:
questions.solution_md: Soda lime is NaOH with CaO — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the laboratory preparation of ethyne from calcium carbide: (a) why is the water added drop by drop? (b) why is ethyne collected over water? (c) why does the gas often smell of garlic?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The reaction is fast and gives out a lot of heat; adding water slowly controls the rate. answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md:
Three gases A, B and C are methane, ethene and ethyne, but not necessarily in that order. A does not decolourise bromine water. One molecule of B adds one molecule of bromine. One molecule of C adds two molecules of bromine.

(a) Identify A, B and C, giving a reason for each. [3]

(b) Write balanced equations for (i) the reaction of B with bromine and (ii) the complete hydrogenation of C. (iii) Name the catalyst used in (ii). [3]

(c) (i) Calculate the volume of hydrogen, at the same temperature and pressure, needed to convert 20 cm³ of C completely into ethane. (ii) Calculate the mass of bromine that reacts with 0.56 g of B. (C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80) [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A is methane: it is saturated and cannot add bromine. B is ethene: one C=C bond adds one Br₂. C is ethyne: one C≡C bond adds two Br₂.

(b) (i) $\ce{C2H4 + Br2 -> C2H4Br2}$ (ii) $\ce{C2H2 + 2H2 -> C2H6}$ (iii) Nickel (at about 300 °C).

(c) (i) 1 volume of ethyne needs 2 volumes of hydrogen: $20 \times 2 = 40$ cm³. (ii) Moles of ethene $= \frac{0.56}{28} = 0.02$; mass of bromine $= 0.02 \times 160 = 3.2$ g.
